The Queens Die; Bharata's Conquest

Stories from the Ramayana

The Queens Die; Bharata's Conquest

Farewell to the three queens — and Bharata's victory in the west

In everyday English — Uttara Kanda, sargas 99–102

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is a story in two parts — a farewell, and a victory. First Ayodhya bids farewell to its three queens. Then Bharata journeys west and founds two new cities. Where there is sorrow, read slowly; where the journey and the new cities come, let hope into your voice.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Rama calm, Bharata humble, Gargya grave.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sargas 99–102 — the death of the three queens and their last rites, the message from Kekaya, Bharata's march west, victory over the Gandharvas, and the founding of Takshashila and Pushkalavati. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — king of Ayodhya. Warm dark-brown skin, a plain golden crown, never a peacock feather. He rules by dharma.

Bharata — Rama's younger brother, son of Kaikeyi. Like Rama, a little lighter in complexion. His elder brother's command is his dharma.

Lakshmana and Shatrughna — Rama's younger brothers, beside Bharata in every sorrow and every task.

Kausalya — Rama's mother, King Dasharatha's eldest queen.

Kaikeyi — Bharata's mother, daughter of the king of Kekaya.

Sumitra — mother of Lakshmana and Shatrughna.

Mandavi — Bharata's wife, mother of Taksha and Pushkala.

Taksha and Pushkala — Bharata's two sons. Taksha the elder, Pushkala the younger.

Yudhajit — king of Kekaya, Kaikeyi's brother, Bharata's maternal uncle.

Gargya — Yudhajit's guru, who came to Ayodhya bearing his message.

Vasishtha — the family guru of Ayodhya, present at every rite.

1 · The Years Pass in Ayodhya · · THE YEARS PASS IN AYODHYA

After the victory over Ravana, Rama became king of Ayodhya. There was happiness in the kingdom — grain in the fields, peace in the city, people busy at their own work.

But time waits for no one. Year after year went by — very many years. Even in Rama's hair, grey began to show, little by little.

In the palace lived the three queens — Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. Now they had grown old. They no longer walked about the palace as before — mostly they sat in their rooms, their minds given to prayer and worship.

Every day Rama went to meet them — he touched their feet and asked after them. Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna too let no service to the queens fall short.

Kausalya would sometimes say — “Rama, you are a king — but to me you are still the same little Rama.”

Rama would smile and say — “Mother, being king is my work — being your son is my true name.”

Ayodhya had everything — but one thing everyone knew and no one said: the queens were old now, and after old age, the time of farewell does come.

Pause and think — Rama is a king — but before his mothers he is still a son. Can a person be a king and a son at the same time? And when parents grow old — is serving them only a duty, or is it love as well?

2 · The Queens Die · · THE QUEENS DIE

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of the death of the three queens. Elders, please read it gently.

Time passed — and the day everyone feared also came.

One by one, the three queens passed away. First Kausalya — Rama's mother, who had given birth to Rama. Then Kaikeyi — Bharata's mother. Then Sumitra — mother of Lakshmana and Shatrughna.

Sorrow fell over Ayodhya. The palace was silent — no drums sounded, no laughter rang in the court. People walked slowly and spoke softly.

Rama sat in silence. He was a king — but that day he was only a son whose mother was no more. Bharata sat beside Rama and held his hand. Lakshmana and Shatrughna sat close by too — the four brothers together, in one shared sorrow.

Bharata said softly — “Brother, our mothers have gone — but their blessings are with us.”

Rama said — “Yes, Bharata. A mother goes — but the values a mother gives never go.”

The people of the city stood outside the palace too — silently, heads bowed. Everyone held the three queens as their own — Kausalya as Rama's mother, Kaikeyi as Bharata's mother, Sumitra as the mother of Lakshmana and Shatrughna — but for Ayodhya, all three were mothers to all.

Pause and think — The three queens went one by one — and the four brothers sat together. Is sitting together in sorrow also a kind of service? And when someone goes — what goes with them, and what stays behind with us?

3 · The Last Rites · · THE LAST RITES

Then Vasishtha came — the family guru of Ayodhya. He said — “The last rites of the queens will be performed as is proper — as is done for the queens of the royal house.”

The four brothers performed the rites together. With ritual and mantras, with full honour, the queens were bid farewell. The priests chanted mantras, lamps were lit, and water was offered on the bank of the Sarayu.

It is said — the queens met King Dasharatha in heaven. Dasharatha had gone long before — and now his three queens too had reached him.

Vasishtha said — “Rama, your mothers lived by dharma and left by dharma. Their names will always be spoken with respect in Ayodhya.”

After the rites, the palace slowly returned to its work — but the queens' rooms stayed empty. No one could take their place — and no one tried.

Rama gave gifts in the queens' names — to brahmins, to the poor, to hermitages. That was another way of farewell — doing good in the name of one who has gone.

Pause and think — The last rites are a matter of sorrow — but they are also a matter of honour. Is bidding someone farewell with honour a way of remembering them? And giving gifts — is doing good in the name of one who has gone like keeping them alive?

4 · A Message from Kekaya · · A MESSAGE FROM KEKAYA

Some time later a guest came to Ayodhya — Gargya. He was the guru of Yudhajit, king of Kekaya — and he had come bearing Yudhajit's message.

Yudhajit — Kaikeyi's brother, Bharata's maternal uncle — was the king of Kekaya. He had sent gifts for Rama — wealth, jewels, and respect from his kingdom.

Gargya said — “King Rama, Yudhajit, king of Kekaya, sends his greetings. And he has said one thing more — please hear it.”

Gargya told them — in the west, on both banks of the river Sindhu, there is a beautiful land — the land of the Gandharvas. There are trees laden with fruit, meadows full of flowers, and the river's water is pure.

“But that land is under the Gandharvas,” Gargya said — “they give it to no one else. Yudhajit says — that land is worth winning, and winning it is work fit for Bharata.”

Rama listened — and began to think. The land of the Gandharvas — beautiful, rich, and as yet in no one's hands.

Pause and think — Yudhajit sends a message — but in the message there is not only news, there is also a suggestion. Is listening to advice from far away also a king's work? And on hearing of a beautiful land — what comes to mind first, its people, or its riches?

5 · Rama's Command · · RAMA'S COMMAND

Rama called Bharata to the court. Bharata came — and stood before Rama with bowed head.

Rama said — “Bharata, go west. Conquer the land of the Gandharvas. Your two sons will go with you — Taksha and Pushkala. Gargya will stay with you — he knows the way.”

Bharata asked nothing — neither why, nor how. His elder brother's command was enough for him. He bowed his head — “As you command, brother.”

Rama said further — “Taksha and Pushkala are grown now. Let them go with you — they will see war, and they will also learn the work of kings. The land that is won will be their kingdom.”

Bharata's wife Mandavi bid farewell to her two sons — Taksha and Pushkala. A mother's heart — her sons were going far away — but this is the dharma of princes.

Mandavi said — “Go, my sons. Go with your father — and keep your uncle Rama's name high.”

The army was readied — chariots, horses, foot soldiers, and stores of grain along with them. Bharata took command of the army — and marched west.

Pause and think — Rama sends Bharata — and with him Bharata's sons too. Is sending the sons along only preparation for war — or is it also teaching them to become kings? And Bharata asks nothing — is obeying a command also a kind of wisdom?

6 · By the River Sindhu · · BY THE RIVER SINDHU

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of a battle that lasted seven nights. Elders, please read it gently.

Bharata's army marched west — through mountains, across plains, crossing rivers. Their uncle Yudhajit joined them too, bringing his own army.

At last they reached the bank of the river Sindhu. The Sindhu — a great river, its water spread far and wide. On both its banks lay the land of the Gandharvas — green trees, meadows of flowers, and the Gandharvas' cities.

The Gandharvas fought — they did not wish to give up their land. The war went on — one night, two nights — for seven nights the war went on.

On the seventh night Bharata loosed the Samvarta weapon — the weapon of Time, which nothing could stop. After that the Gandharva army could not hold — they were defeated.

The war ended. The land of the Gandharvas was now in Bharata's hands — on this bank of the Sindhu too, and on the far bank as well.

Pause and think — The war lasted seven nights — and then a single weapon ended it. Is winning a war itself victory — or is what is built after the war the true victory? And the Gandharvas fought for their land — is there something worth hearing even in the side that loses?

7 · Two Cities, Two Princes · · TWO CITIES, TWO PRINCES

After the war, Bharata took charge of the land. He founded two cities — one on each bank of the Sindhu.

On this bank of the Sindhu — the eastern bank — Takshashila was founded. That city was given to Taksha — Bharata's elder son.

On the far bank — the western bank — Pushkalavati was founded. That city was given to Pushkala — Bharata's younger son.

Both cities were built beautifully — high walls, wide roads, markets, temples and palaces. People came to settle — traders, craftsmen, farmers.

Bharata said to both his sons — “This city is your kingdom. Rule it not by the sword — but by dharma. If the people are happy, a king's name rises on its own.”

Taksha became king of Takshashila — and Pushkala king of Pushkalavati. The two brothers lived in their own cities — on the two banks of the Sindhu, facing each other.

It is said — Takshashila later became a great centre of learning, where people came from far and wide to study. And Pushkalavati came to be called the capital of the Gandhara land.

Pause and think — Two banks of one river — and two brothers, two kings. Does the river divide them — or join them? And when Bharata gives his sons cities, what is he giving them — land, or responsibility?

8 · Bharata Returns · · BHARATA RETURNS

Having seated both his sons in their kingdoms, Bharata returned to Ayodhya. It was a long journey — from west to east, from the bank of the Sindhu to the bank of the Sarayu.

In Ayodhya, Rama welcomed Bharata. Bharata touched Rama's feet — and told him the whole story: the message from Kekaya, the seven nights of war, the Samvarta weapon, and the two new cities.

Rama said — “Bharata, what you have done is a king's work. Taksha and Pushkala are kings now — and the name of Rama's line will live on both banks of the Sindhu.”

Bharata said — “Brother, all this happened by your command. I only walked — you showed the way.”

That day Ayodhya felt festive again — but without the queens, the festival was not as before. Rama knew — the queens had gone, but their blessings had now reached the banks of the Sindhu — in two new cities, in two new kings.

And so the story of Bharata's victory ends — begun in farewell, finished in two new cities.

Pause and think — Bharata returned victorious — but he gives the credit for the victory to Rama. Is giving away the credit also part of victory? And the queens are no more — but are they still alive in the work of their sons and grandsons?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sargas 99–102.

The Queens' Death — Sarga 99

In time, Kausalya and Kaikeyi die and meet Dasharatha in heaven — this is in the closing passages of the Uttara Kanda. Sumitra's death is held to belong to the same time — the brothers performed the last rites of all three queens as is proper.

The Message from Kekaya — Sarga 100

Yudhajit, king of Kekaya, sending his guru Gargya to Ayodhya with gifts and a message; the description of the Gandharva land spread on both banks of the Sindhu, full of fruits and flowers; Rama commanding Bharata to go west with his sons — this is in this passage.

Victory over the Gandharvas — Sarga 101

Bharata marching west with the army; his uncle Yudhajit joining him; seven nights of war by the Sindhu; Bharata loosing the Samvarta weapon and the defeat of the Gandharvas — this is in sarga 101.

Two Cities — Sarga 102

Taksha made king in Takshashila and Pushkala made king in Pushkalavati; Bharata seating his sons in their kingdoms and returning to Ayodhya — this is in sarga 102.

About the Sarga Numbers

The number of sargas in the Uttara Kanda differs between printed editions — in some editions this passage is printed at a slightly different sarga number. This book follows the longer numbering, sargas 99–102; the story is the same.

Takshashila and Pushkalavati — About the Places

Takshashila is traditionally identified with the Taxila region of today, and Pushkalavati with the Charsadda region of today — these are traditional identifications, not facts proven by archaeology. The story places Takshashila on the eastern bank of the Sindhu and Pushkalavati on the western bank.

About the Pictures

No body is shown in this book's pictures — the queens' death is told only in words, and the pictures show the brothers seated in mourning. The battle picture too has no blood or wounds — the armies stand by the riverbank.

What Happens Next

After Bharata's return, Rama's rule goes on for many more years — the next stories of the Uttara Kanda are in the coming books of this series.
